extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners; patent prosecutors and applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether claim additional elements amount to an 'inventive concept' (i.e., whether the claim as a whole is 'significantly more' than a judicial exception) under Step 2B of the Alice/Mayo framework in the MPEP.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B: Whether additional elements contribute an 'inventive concept'
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2B asks: Does the claim recite additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should identify additional elements beyond the judicial exception(s) and evaluate those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they contribute an inventive concept (i.e., amount to significantly more). This evaluation is made with respect to the considerations the Supreme Court identified as relevant and discussed in MPEP § 2106.05(a)-(h). The evaluation is not a weighing test; focus on the significance of the additional elements relative to the invention and whether the claim as a whole encompasses an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify additional elements beyond the judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should answer Step 2B by first identifying whether there are any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry over the identification of additional element(s) from Step 2A Prong Two and consult the specification when identifying and characterizing additional elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate additional elements individually and in combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the identified additional elements both individually and in combination to determine whether they contribute an inventive concept (i.e., are 'significantly more' than the exception).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether an inventive concept may be found in a non-conventional or non-generic arrangement of additional elements when assessed together (e.g., BASCOM: remote filtering tool at a particular location with customizable features). Analyze the claim 'as a whole' and as an 'ordered combination,' and do not ignore specific claim requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carry over and re-evaluate Step 2A Prong Two conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should carry over conclusions from Step 2A Prong Two on the considerations discussed in MPEP §§ 2106.05(a)-(c), (e), (f) and (h).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-evaluate any additional element or combination previously considered 'insignificant extra-solution activity' under MPEP § 2106.05(g), because a finding that an element is unconventional or more than well-understood, routine, conventional activity may change the Step 2B outcome. Also evaluate whether any additional element or combination merely appends well-understood, routine, conventional activities specified at a high level of generality per MPEP § 2106.05(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-by-claim analysis (do not conflate similar claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should examine each claim for eligibility separately, based on the particular elements recited therein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should not be judged to automatically stand or fall with similar claims in an application; a dependent claim may be eligible due to additional elements even if the independent claim is ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B outcomes: Pathway C eligibility or 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the exception, the claim is eligible (Step 2B: YES) at Pathway C; if not, the claim is not patent-eligible (Step 2B: NO) and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a claim is ineligible, see MPEP § 2106.07 for guidance on how to formulate an ineligibility rejection. The eligibility analysis is concluded at Step 2B once the determination is made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements to the functioning of a computer or other technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the claim 'purport(s) to improve the functioning of the computer itself' or 'any other technology or technical field.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consideration looks for a technological solution to a technological problem. The specification should provide a technical explanation of how to implement the asserted improvement such that one of ordinary skill would recognize it. Conclusory assertions of improvement without necessary detail are insufficient. The claim must reflect the disclosed improvement (may include components or steps providing the improvement), though the claim need not literally recite the improvement phrase. Evaluate the claim 'as an ordered combination' and avoid oversimplifying. Improvement consideration overlaps with other considerations (particular machine, mere instructions to apply an exception). The judicial exception alone cannot provide the improvement; additional elements or their combination can.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-functionality improvement requires computer-limited scope
rubrics_metrics.description: For a method claim to improve computer functionality, the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim must be limited to computer implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim whose entire scope can be performed mentally or without a computer cannot be said to improve computer technology (see Synopsys; RecogniCorp). Claims that cover both computer and non-computer embodiments cannot be treated as improving computer technology unless limited to computer implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples that may or may not show improvements in computer-functionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have listed specific examples that may show an improvement in computer functionality and examples that may not be sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples that may show improvements include (i) modification of hyperlink protocol to produce hybrid webpages (DDR Holdings), (ii) inventive distribution of functionality within a network to filter Internet content (BASCOM), (iii) method of rendering halftone images, (iv) distributed network architecture reducing congestion (Amdocs/Openet), (v) programmable memory system configurable by processor type (Visual Memory), (vi) technical details for transmitting images over cellular networks or appending classification info (TLI Communications), (vii) particular server structure for organized digital images (TLI Communications), (viii) particular programming/design to create menus (Ameranth), (ix) methods generating security profiles improving virus protection (Finjan), (x) improved selectable application summary UIs (Core Wireless), (xi) specific interface/implementation for 3D spreadsheets (Data Engine), (xii) specific method of restricting software operation within a license (Ancora). Examples that may NOT be sufficient include (i) generating restaurant menus with functionally claimed features (Ameranth), (ii) accelerating analysis solely from a general-purpose computer (FairWarning), (iii) mere automation of manual processes using generic computers (Credit Acceptance; LendingTree), (iv) recording/transmitting/archiving digital images with conventional tech (TLI Communications), (v) affixing a barcode without technical details (Secured Mail Solutions), (vi) instructions to display two sets of information without how to achieve result (Interval Licensing), (vii) improving information stored in a database (BSG Tech), (viii) arranging transactional information on a GUI to help traders process faster (Trading Technologies). Use these as illustrative guidance, not exhaustive rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements to other technologies or technical fields (non-computer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of improvements is relevant regardless of the technology; improvements in other technologies may demonstrate patent eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have found eligibility where claims improve non-computer technologies (e.g., improved method of preserving hepatocytes (Rapid Litigation Management), computerized rubber molding press improvements (Diehr), new telephone/server combinations (TLI), advances in downloading content for streaming (Affinity Labs), improved digital data compression (DDR), components generating new data (Electric Power Group)). However, an improvement in the abstract idea itself (e.g., improved business process or economic concept) is not an improvement in technology. The improvement should be a particular way to achieve a desired outcome and not merely the idea of the solution.
